title: Forest-Village Stays in the Dooars: Where to Sleep
meta_description: Where to stay in the Dooars forests: Murti and Lataguri for Gorumara, Chilapata's Mendabari lodge, Jhalong's river camp and Bindu homestays, with costs.
summary: Sleep beside the forest, not on the highway. Murti's riverside forest corporation cottages and Lataguri's homestays serve Gorumara; Mendabari at Chilapata sits deep in elephant forest near Jaldapara; Jhalong's river camp and Bindu's homestays face Bhutan across the Jaldhaka. Expect ₹1,200–2,000 per person in homestays and ₹1,800–4,000 a room in forest lodges.

sections.heading: Why sleep in a forest village
paras: Most visitors to the Dooars sleep in a resort on the Lataguri highway, drive to a watchtower for an hour and drive back. The forest is something they visit. Stay instead in a forest village or a forest corporation camp at its edge and the forest comes to you: elephants trumpet across the river at night, peafowl call at dawn, and the walk to breakfast passes the prints of something large that crossed the compound before you woke.

It is usually cheaper too. Homestays in forest villages charge ₹1,200–2,000 per person with dinner and breakfast, and the West Bengal Forest Development Corporation (WBFDC) runs cottages, tents and lodges at Murti, Lataguri, Dhupjhora, Suntalekhola, Jhalong and Mendabari for ₹1,500–4,000 a room. What you give up is the swimming pool and the television. What you gain is the reason you came.

A good plan uses two or three bases over a week rather than one. Sleep two nights near Gorumara, two near Jaldapara and two at Buxa or Jayanti, and add Jhalong or Samsing if you have time. Each move is two to three hours by car or train, short enough to arrive for an afternoon safari or a sunset on a riverbed.

sections.heading: Murti and Lataguri, for Gorumara
paras: Lataguri is the village where Gorumara's safari counters are, so it is the practical base, with dozens of homestays and the WBFDC Lataguri Eco-Tourism Centre. The trouble is the main road: trucks at night and loud resort parties on winter weekends. Choose a homestay on a side lane or towards the forest edge, and ask whether the house cooks its own meals, which is the best sign.

Murti, 15–20 minutes away where the Murti river leaves the hills, is the quieter choice. The WBFDC's Murti Banani Eco-Tourism Centre has cottages and tents on the riverbank, between Gorumara and Chapramari, and evenings on the wide stony bed are the best hour of the day. You will need a car to reach the Lataguri counter, ₹600–1,000 for the trip. Dhupjhora's forest corporation elephant camp, nearby, lets you watch the camp elephants bathed in the river in the morning; it has only a few rooms. Kalipur eco village, a small camp inside the forest on the Lataguri side, is the most remote option, with a watchtower close by.

sections.heading: Chilapata, for Jaldapara and the corridor
paras: Chilapata is a dense forest east of Jaldapara and part of the elephant corridor linking it with Buxa Tiger Reserve. The WBFDC's Mendabari Jungle Lodge sits in the forest here, 20–30 minutes from Madarihat and 10–15 km from Hasimara station. It is one of the quietest places to sleep in the Dooars: no highway, no town, only the forest and the night sounds.

From here you can take Chilapata's own jeep safaris, which pass the brick ruins of Nalraja Garh, and reach Jaldapara's morning slots by car. Meals are simple and served at fixed times, about ₹500 a person a day. Bring a torch and do not walk outside the compound after dark; elephants pass through. Since the Hollong lodge inside Jaldapara burnt down in June 2024, Mendabari is the closest thing to a night inside Jaldapara's forest that we can recommend.

sections.heading: Jhalong and Bindu, on the Bhutan border
paras: The Jaldhaka valley climbs north from the plains near Chalsa to the Bhutan border, and for most of its length the river is the frontier: India on one bank, Bhutanese forest on the other. Jhalong, about 100 km from Siliguri, is a small settlement built around a hydroelectric power station, with the WBFDC's Jholung River Camp and a handful of homestays. Dawn on the shingle brings river birds and mist on the Bhutan hills.

Bindu, 10–15 km further up, is the last Indian village on the road, at the barrage that diverts the Jaldhaka to the Jhalong power station. Most visitors come for an hour. Spend a night in a Bindu homestay, at ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals, and you have the valley to yourself once the day cars leave. Shared jeeps run between Jhalong and Bindu a few times a day; a car costs ₹800–1,200 return. There is no border crossing for travellers here.

sections.heading: Buxa, Jayanti and the hill villages
paras: Two other kinds of village stay round out the Dooars, and both are as cheap as it gets.

In Buxa Tiger Reserve, Dukpa families in Buxa village and at Lepchakha, higher on the ridge, run simple homestays reached only on foot, by the 5 km stone path from Santalabari. Rooms are basic, bathrooms sometimes shared and power unreliable, but the food is home-cooked and the dawn view from Lepchakha over the plains is one of the best in the region. Down on the plain, Jayanti has a cluster of homestays on the edge of its huge riverbed, a base for the Mahakal cave and Pokhri lake walks and for Buxa safaris. Both charge ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals.

In the first hills above Chalsa, Samsing's tea garden village has homestays at about 900 m, three to five degrees cooler than the plains, and the WBFDC's Suntaleykhola Eco-Tourism Centre sits 5 km beyond, across a hanging footbridge over a stream from Neora Valley National Park. These are the places to sleep in April and May, when the plains are hot, coming down to Gorumara for safaris an hour away.

sections.heading: Booking forest corporation rooms
paras: WBFDC cottages, tents and lodges are booked online on the corporation's own site, which lists each property, its room types and its current tariff; pay at the time of booking and carry the same ID you booked with. Most properties have only a handful of rooms, and winter weekends, Christmas week and the Durga Puja holidays sell out weeks or months ahead. Meals at these camps are usually charged separately at fixed rates.

Safari slots are booked on a different forest department system, so book both and check that the dates match. Many camps close or restrict bookings during the monsoon closure, roughly 16 June to 15 September, and some were affected by the October 2025 floods. Tariffs and policies change; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Homestay manners and safety
paras: Forest-village stays are homes and working villages, not hotels. A few habits make them work for everyone.
list: Tell hosts your arrival time and meal needs early; they shop for food in the morning.
Carry cash in small notes; most forest villages have no ATM and patchy mobile data.
Keep inside the compound after dark, use a torch and never walk to the river at night.
Never approach or follow elephants, even from a vehicle, and keep away from fresh dung on paths.
Keep noise and music down; sound carries far in the forest and disturbs neighbours and animals.
Take your rubbish back to town; villages have little waste collection.

faqs.q: Where should we stay for Gorumara, Lataguri or Murti?
faqs.a: Lataguri if you want convenience: the safari counters are there and homestays cost ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals. Murti if you want quiet: forest corporation cottages on the riverbank, 15–20 minutes away, at ₹1,800–4,000 a room. From Murti you need a car to the Lataguri counter.

faqs.q: How do we book WBFDC forest lodges?
faqs.a: Online on the West Bengal Forest Development Corporation's own website, which lists each property's rooms and current tariff. Pay at booking and carry the same ID. Rooms are few, so book weeks ahead for winter weekends and holidays. Safari slots are booked separately on the forest department's system.

faqs.q: Is Mendabari Jungle Lodge at Chilapata worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want quiet. The forest corporation lodge sits inside the Chilapata forest, 20–30 minutes from Madarihat, with rooms at about ₹2,500 and simple meals at about ₹500 a day. Elephants pass at night, so stay in the compound after dark. It suits a Jaldapara and Chilapata trip well.

Yes. A few village homestays at Bindu, the last Indian village up the Jaldhaka valley, charge about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with dinner and breakfast. Rooms are simple. Most visitors come only for an hour from Jhalong, so evenings are very quiet. Carry cash and expect weak mobile signal.

faqs.q: Is it safe to stay in forest villages in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Yes, with sensible care. Stay inside your compound after dark, use a torch, keep away from riverbeds at dusk and never approach elephants, which cause most serious incidents here. Follow your host's advice. After heavy rain, avoid river crossings, as levels rise fast.

faqs.q: Are forest lodges in the Dooars open in the monsoon?
faqs.a: Many close or restrict bookings during the park closure, roughly 16 June to 15 September, and some camps near rivers were affected by the October 2025 floods. Homestays outside the parks often stay open. Check current status before you travel and confirm directly with the property.

faqs.q: What is the Jholung River Camp?
faqs.a: A forest corporation camp at Jhalong in the Jaldhaka valley, on the river with Bhutan's forested hills on the far bank. Rooms cost about ₹2,500–3,500 indicatively. It is a base for river birding, the drive to Bindu and quiet evenings, about three hours from NJP via Malbazar and Chalsa.

faqs.q: Do forest corporation camps serve food?
faqs.a: Yes, usually simple fixed menus of rice, dal, vegetables, eggs or chicken at set times, charged separately at about ₹500–700 per person a day. Tell staff your arrival time. There are rarely other places to eat nearby, so carry snacks and water if you arrive late.

faqs.q: Is Hollong lodge in Jaldapara available?
faqs.a: No. Hollong, the wooden forest lodge inside Jaldapara, was gutted by fire on 18 June 2024 and we have not confirmed any reopening. Stay at Madarihat or at the Mendabari lodge in Chilapata instead, and check with the forest department before paying for anything advertised under the Hollong name.
